query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising to provide effective antiballistic capability because of their superior mechanical properties. However, the twinning-active Cantor alloy is found less ballistic resistant, compared with its Mn-free companion. It is unclear how the HEAs resist ballistic impact and why Mn does not benefit the ballistic resistance. Here, we used molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the ballistic resistances of CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi and elucidate underlying mechanisms. It is shown that the alloys’ ballistic resistances dominantly benefit from active dislocations generated at higher strain rates. Stronger atomic bonding and higher dislocation densities make the CrFeCoNi easier to be strain hardened with elevated toughness to resist high-speed deformation, while weaker atomic bonding and easier occurrence of dislocation tangling make CrMnFeCoNi less resistant to failure under ballistic impact. This work helps better understand the antiballistic behavior of HEAs and guide the design of armor and energy-absorption materials. Higher strain rate induces more active dislocations, benefiting the ballistic resistances of high-entropy alloys.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their mechanical properties, such as strength, ductility, and plasticity. Earlier studies have explored the effects of composition, microstructure, and processing conditions on these properties. Recently, there has been a shift towards investigating the dynamic behavior of these alloys across different temperatures and strain rates. The trend suggests that researchers are moving towards a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing the mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys.
